title: Claims & Argument Structure — Skill Check
description: Identify the main claim, supporting claims, and how the argument’s parts build on one another.
subject: rla
author: Chee Skool
reviewNotes: Unseen independent check; no hints, retries, or guided scaffolding.

questions.prompt: What is the committee’s main claim?

options.text: All students should stop driving to campus.
options.whyWrong: The proposal is a limited bicycle-storage trial, not a ban on driving.

options.text: A small secure bicycle-storage trial could remove a cycling barrier without seriously reducing parking.
Bus passes are harmful to campus transportation.
options.whyWrong: The committee supports bus discounts as a separate option.

options.text: Every bicycle theft happened in the east lot.
options.whyWrong: Fourteen of eighteen reported thefts involved east-side racks, not all thefts.

explanation.whyCorrect: This choice best matches the argument: A small secure bicycle-storage trial could remove a cycling barrier without seriously reducing parking.
explanation.quickTip: Track the exact claim, evidence, and reasoning before judging the argument.

questions.prompt: Which statement functions as a supporting claim rather than the main claim?

options.text: The college should convert every parking space into bicycle storage.
Students who drive should receive free bus passes.
options.whyWrong: This is not the committee’s proposal.

options.text: The east lot has enough unused capacity to host the trial without creating a serious shortage.
The trial should last exactly one year because one year is always sufficient.
options.whyWrong: The one-year period is proposed, but this is not argued as a universal rule.

explanation.whyCorrect: This choice best matches the argument: The east lot has enough unused capacity to host the trial without creating a serious shortage.
explanation.quickTip: Track the exact claim, evidence, and reasoning before judging the argument.

questions.prompt: Which sequence best represents the committee’s argument chain?

options.text: Storage concern → theft/weather evidence → secure area addresses concern → parking data limits tradeoff → one-year trial
Parking shortage → bus discounts → bicycle theft → permanent removal of car spaces
options.whyWrong: This reverses and mixes the argument’s steps.

options.text: Bicycle theft → all students must cycle → parking is unnecessary → trial is permanent
options.whyWrong: The passage makes none of those broad claims.

options.text: Weather exposure → buses are ineffective → east lot is full → cancel the trial

explanation.whyCorrect: This choice best matches the argument: Storage concern → theft/weather evidence → secure area addresses concern → parking data limits tradeoff → one-year trial
explanation.quickTip: Track the exact claim, evidence, and reasoning before judging the argument.

questions.prompt: Why does the paragraph about morning parking appear after the theft and survey evidence?

options.text: To introduce an unrelated topic before returning to bicycles
options.whyWrong: Parking is a direct tradeoff created by the proposal.

options.text: To prove theft reports were inaccurate
options.whyWrong: The parking data do not challenge the theft records.

options.text: To replace the main claim with a new claim about cars
options.whyWrong: The main proposal remains bicycle storage.

options.text: To address a likely cost of the proposal after establishing the problem it is meant to solve

explanation.whyCorrect: This choice best matches the argument: To address a likely cost of the proposal after establishing the problem it is meant to solve
explanation.quickTip: Track the exact claim, evidence, and reasoning before judging the argument.

questions.prompt: Which statement is a supporting claim the committee uses to defend the bicycle-storage trial?

options.text: Every student should travel by bicycle.
options.whyWrong: The committee proposes one transportation option and never claims everyone should cycle.

options.text: Bus discounts should be eliminated.
options.whyWrong: The committee supports bus discounts as a separate option.

options.text: Existing parking counts suggest the east lot can give up 12 spaces without a serious shortage.
The bicycle area must become permanent after one year.
options.whyWrong: The committee calls for reviewing trial evidence before any permanent change.

explanation.whyCorrect: This supporting claim connects the parking-count evidence to the committee’s larger claim that the trial can occur without a serious parking shortage.
explanation.quickTip: A supporting claim helps carry the main claim and is backed by its own evidence.

questions.prompt: Which description best captures the structure of the full argument?

options.text: A personal preference followed by unrelated statistics and no response to objections
options.whyWrong: The passage uses claim-specific evidence and responses.

options.text: A claim that secure storage is perfect, followed by a demand for permanent construction
options.whyWrong: The committee proposes a limited trial and later review.

options.text: A targeted proposal supported by problem evidence, followed by responses to parking and alternative-policy objections, then a measured trial plan
A comparison of two bicycle brands followed by a parking survey

explanation.whyCorrect: This choice best matches the argument: A targeted proposal supported by problem evidence, followed by responses to parking and alternative-policy objections, then a measured trial plan
explanation.quickTip: Track the exact claim, evidence, and reasoning before judging the argument.

curriculum.learningObjective: Identify the main claim, supporting claims, and how the argument’s parts build on one another.
